chapter_title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teacher
chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic dialogue frame and a moral-theological apologetic about God as judge. It contains no systematic cosmological-correspondential mapping (the diagnostic of the oldest substrate). The explicit Gospel/NT vector appears in the “saviour has said” quotation and in the term “gehenna,” marking Christian overlay. The remainder reads as later didactic/pastoral reasoning rather than the impersonal, structural teaching core.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic narrative setup (“Once again… it happened one time”), sectarian character introduction, and “apostle” title mark the editorial hagiographic frame.
Dialogue attribution (“The apostle speaks…”) and Q&A staging function as compilation frame rather than cosmological exposition.
Question-in-dialogue within the staged encounter; no impersonal systematic teaching, only narrative prompt.
Continues the dialogue frame with address and rhetorical correction; “Then says the apostle…” is a classic framing attribution.
Ethical/polemical argument using civic-judge imagery (lashes, racks, sword) aimed at moral reasoning, not cosmos→cosmos correspondence; reads as later apologetic discourse.
Didactic explanation about limiting evil and punishing sinners; second-person argumentative teaching without cosmological architecture.
Direct audience-address/imperative (“pay attention to this”) and moral illustration of judge not harming the innocent—application-style rhetoric.
Moral causality argument (“brings… upon his own head,” recompense for goodness) in homiletic style; no distinct cosmological system description.
Generalizing move (“this also is the way of God… judge of souls”) continues the ethical analogy; devil/truth language used for exhortative moral framing, not a structured cosmological map.

Explicit NT entry vector: “Even as the saviour has said” followed by a Gospel-style saying (treasure/heart; Mt 6 per apparatus). This marks later Christian overlay regardless of how well it fits Manichaean themes.
Use of “gehenna” (Gospel/NT eschatological term) indicates Christian overlay diction rather than the oldest substrate’s cosmological register.
Reward/kingdom/heirs/life eternal vocabulary aligns with NT soteriological idiom; “kingdom of light” is Manichaean-sounding, but the surrounding phraseology reads as NT-mediated overlay.
Concluding moral-theological summary (“God… is a judge… limits the evil”) in exhortative/apologetic voice; no citation formula, but still not the impersonal cosmological substrate.
